note: The ordered quality-gate catalogue. ops/quality/run-gates.ps1 executes exactly this, in this order, and writes one evidence record per stage. A developer and CI call the same runner; nothing here is a CI-only concern.

placeholders.{evidenceRoot}: the evidence directory for this run
placeholders.{stageDir}: per-stage evidence directory for this run

orderRationale: plan.md section 7.1. Cheap and static first so a typo is reported in seconds rather than after a four-minute build; the database-bound stages next; the cross-cutting validators after the artifacts they read; the destructive rehearsal last, so nothing runs after it that could need restoring. Every stage reports separately: a red stage is never masked by a green neighbour.

stages.name: performance-smoke
stages.title: Performance smoke with recorded percentiles and telemetry

commands.label: boot a disposable seeded application, run the smoke, tear the whole thing down

stages.scopeNote: REWRITTEN IN PHASE 43. This stage had never passed: its only command invoked run-smoke.ps1 with no -TargetBaseUrl and no -SessionCookie, which the harness correctly REFUSES -- and the runner scored that refusal as a failure. A gate that cannot pass is not a gate. The command now goes through a wrapper that supplies the missing orchestration: it creates a disposable database, boots the application against it on ports 4501/4502 (clear of shadow-parity's 4401-4403), loads tests/performance/dataset.sql, signs in as the seeded performance identity, runs the smoke, and drops the database in a finally block. It refuses to touch any database not on its disposable-name check, and it builds nothing -- a gate that compiles its own subject can report green about code it compiled rather than code it was given. The 'never skips' property is unchanged and now structural: every failure path exits 1 with the reason, and there is no branch that reports a pass it did not measure.
stages.note: The performance identity's password is generated per run and never committed. Only its bcrypt hash reaches dataset.sql, and the database holding that hash is dropped at teardown -- including on failure -- so no usable credential survives the run. This replaced a deliberately INVALID hash that made the stage unwirable; see the note at the users insert in dataset.sql.

stages.name: migration-verification
stages.title: Migration verification against a disposable database
stages.rationale: Runs the full V1-V11 bundle on a throwaway database that has just had the whole chain applied, and proves the development database was not touched by comparing its verification bundle before and after. Expected counts are NOT hardcoded here: ops/flyway/expected-state.json holds the preBoot and postBoot profiles and verify-schema-state.ps1 selects between them by asking the database whether flyway_schema_history exists, failing if neither matches. This is what stops the pipeline failing on cutover day because a number written before the first Flyway boot no longer describes the database.

create a DISPOSABLE database and apply the whole Flyway chain to it
verification bundle on the disposable database, asserting the profile that database actually is (the whole chain is applied to it, so it asserts postBoot)

the whole Flyway chain applies to a DISPOSABLE database created from empty, and the resulting state matches expected-state.json postBoot -- this is the check that would have caught V20261006110000, whose guard compared rendered constraint DDL that changes with search_path
read-only verification bundle of the development database, AFTER (same profile as BEFORE)
the development database's fingerprint and row counts are identical before and after

stages.name: shadow-parity
stages.title: Shadow-read parity against the frozen legacy runtime
stages.requirement: plan.md Phase 12 steps 1-2 (shadow reads; compare row counts, authorization decisions, status transitions, analytics, finance rollups, exports)
stages.rationale: Compares the frozen NestJS/Prisma implementation against the Spring/PostgreSQL one, each on its own DISPOSABLE database seeded from one file, and reports differences. It is EXPECTED TO FAIL until parity is real: its verdict is evidence, not a target. A comparison that only ever passes is decoration, so the harness asserts nine deliberate perturbations to prove each check can go red.
stages.scopeNote: Bootstraps two runtimes for about two and a half minutes on ports 4401-4403 and releases them on exit; do not run it concurrently with another gate binding those ports. It NEVER touches the firstelement database. The FIRST TWO commands are pure node suites and are ordered before the harness on purpose. They cover the two things the harness itself cannot be trusted to report about: PN-08's verdict (it lived inside this 1,000-line script where no one could exercise it, and examination found its 'generation 1 stayed frozen' conjunct compared `olderGenerations` against itself -- true by construction, and true when no generation-1 row existed), and the snapshot partitioning that FEEDS it. That second one is Phase 43: `olderGenerations` was computed by an inline loop that dropped every displaced generation, so it was structurally ALWAYS empty for an ascending result and a run could not see generation 1 even with generation 1 in the table. Both suites execute the pre-fix logic to prove it was blind, rather than asserting the new behaviour in prose.

commands.label: PN-08 verdict proof, both states, no databases and no runtimes
snapshot generation partitioning, including the pre-fix logic proven blind
legacy-vs-Spring read parity, authorization decisions, status transitions and finance rollups
